title: yoga nidra
hook: the Katha Upanishad speaks of one who stays awake in those who sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the gathering in: the senses drawn into the mind: the rays gather into the sun. Did you move attention through one hand without moving it? Day one thousand twenty-five.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: A night nurse walks a quiet ward at three in the morning. Every bed holds a sleeper. Some breathe slowly. One talks in a dream. One turns over and pulls the blanket up. The nurse is the only one awake, moving from bed to bed, seeing it all, waking no one. The Katha Upanishad has a line that sounds like that ward, but it's describing something inside each sleeper. It says someone stays awake in us while we sleep. On this last day of yoga nidra, we meet the watcher.
screen: `A QUIET WARD AT THREE A.M.` → `EVERY BED HOLDS A SLEEPER.` → `ONE IS AWAKE, WAKING NO ONE.`

segments.voice: The Katha Upanishad is Death's teaching to a boy named Nachiketas, and in its fifth section comes this, in paraphrase. The Person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another, that is the bright one, that is Brahman, that alone is called the deathless. Read it slowly. In the Upanishad's picture, even while we dream, while the mind builds its chariots and roads, something is awake and doing the shaping. The Gita picks up the same image and turns it around. What is night for all beings, Krishna says in chapter two, in that the self-mastered one is awake. And where beings are awake, that is night for the sage who sees. The world's busy daytime is a kind of sleep, and what the world sleeps through, the sage is awake to. Another Upanishad has a word for this one who watches: sakshi, the witness. The Shvetashvatara calls the one God, hidden in all beings, the witness, the one who knows, alone, beyond the qualities. That's where the yoga nidra days have been heading. The Goddess holding Vishnu's sleep. The Mandukya's rooms and the fourth beyond them. The falcon going home. Patanjali calling sleep a movement of the mind. The resolve. The senses gathered in. Read side by side, each can be taken, from a different angle, as pointing toward one thing: rest so deep it looks like sleep, with the witness still awake. Teachers of the practice say it plainly: the body sleeps, and awareness doesn't. Whether that's reached in one session or in a lifetime, the texts set the watcher at the center.
screen: `AWAKE IN THOSE WHO SLEEP.` · `NIGHT FOR ALL BEINGS; THE SAGE IS AWAKE.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.` · `EVERY ANGLE, ONE WATCHER.` · then, large: `THE BODY SLEEPS. AWARENESS DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Lie down if you can, or sit back with eyes closed. Let the body go heavy, one part at a time, the way we practiced yesterday. Let the breath do what it does. Now notice that something is noticing all this. The heaviness, the breath, a sound in the room, a stray thought. Don't try to find the noticer or picture it. Just rest as the one who sees, like the nurse on the ward, waking no one. The bell holds the time.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Deep rest for the body, with the witness, the sakshi, still awake.

Your line: something in you stays awake. Today, once in the middle of something busy, notice for three breaths that something in you is watching it all, the way the nurse watches the ward. Day one thousand twenty-five.

howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta speak of the sakshi, the witness that remains through waking, dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as deep rest for the body with awareness kept awake.

God hidden in all beings, the witness

myth: the Katha Upanishad says nothing in a person is awake during sleep
it speaks of the Person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping desire after desire.
in the Gita, what is night for all beings is where the self-mastered one is awake
Krishna says it in chapter two, and turns it around: where beings are awake is night for the sage.
sakshi means the one who acts
sakshi is the witness, the one who sees.

fork.setup: you're lying deep in rest, the body heavy. a thought drifts past. what do you do?
options: chase it, to see where it goes.
push it away to get back to rest.
notice it, as the one who sees.
fork.reveal: the texts set the witness at the center: the one who sees the thought, the breath and the heavy body, and wakes none of them.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sakshi, witness. The one who sees, awake through waking, dream and sleep.

trapdoor: what you thought: yoga nidra is a way to fall asleep faster.
what it means: it's deep rest for the body with the witness still awake.
what a scholar hears: Katha 5.8 (awake in those who sleep), Gita 2.69, and the sakshi of Shvetashvatara 6.11.

notes: Editor pass: review updated for 1024's new carry; Shvetashvatara 6.11 paraphrase tightened ('the witness, the one who knows, alone, beyond the qualities'); carry changed from a bedtime noticing (repeated 1019's) to noticing the watcher in a busy moment.
Last day of the yoga nidra block (1019–1025); the teach names each day's angle in order. Next block: trataka.
Katha 5.8 paraphrased (ya esha supteshu jagarti kamam kamam purusho nirmimanah...). Max Müller's SBE 15 rendering exists but wasn't quoted because the exact wording wasn't certain.
Gita 2.69 and Shvetashvatara 6.11 (sakshi, cheta, kevalo nirgunash cha) paraphrased; confirm.
'Another Upanishad has a word for this one who watches' is a light framing; confirm it's fair to place Shvetashvatara as later relative to Katha, or cut 'later'.
The night-nurse scene is the script's own image.

Audit: the hook and teach stated the witness as fact in the narrator's voice ('someone stays awake in us'); now attributed to the Upanishad. The block recap no longer claims every text (including the Devi Mahatmya) 'points at the same thing'; it is offered as a reading. Note 5's 'or cut later' refers to wording no longer in the voice.
